10.1002_aenm.202505649: Water governs both reactivity and transport in aqueous batteries, yet the occurrence of distinct free, coordinated, and network‐bound states complicates electrolyte design. Here, a quantitative water‐speciation identification (QWSI) strategy is established to resolve and quantify water populations and to correlate composition with microstructure and function. Aqueous Zn‐I 2 batteries are employed as a model system owing to the high sensitivity of capacity to water‐state distributions. Eliminating free water stabilizes electrophilic iodine species and activates the I 2 /2I + couple to realize a four‐electron conversion that doubles capacity, whereas driving water content too low depletes coordinated and network‐bound water, slows ion transport, and ultimately compromises capacity. The QWSI strategy pinpoints a critical composition at which water resides within hydrogen‐bond networks and cation solvation shells, with no detectable bulk‐like free water. Electrolytes formulated at this composition sustain four‐electron conversion while maintaining high ionic conductivity, reconciling activation of four‐electron conversion with ion transport. Consequently, the Zn//I 2 cells deliver distinct two‐plateau profiles and high reversibility, enabling an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.8% and a specific capacity of 309.1 mAh·g −1 . These findings define molecular control of water‐state distributions as a design principle, while the QWSI strategy provides quantitative descriptors for predictive control of solvation and reactivity across aqueous electrochemistry.
10.1016_j.apenergy.2026.128311: Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), powered by high-purity green hydrogen, represent affordable and sustainable solutions for decarbonizing modern energy systems. In PEMFCs, the multiphase transport properties of bipolar plates (BPs), which depend on their design characteristics, largely determine cell efficiency and longevity. Although unconventional BP designs have been developed to enhance mass transport, their implementation has remained limited to laboratory-scale demonstrations due to the restricted design adaptability and low fabrication resolution of conventional manufacturing routes. Additive manufacturing, with its geometric freedom, enables the fabrication of complex and nonintuitive geometries with fewer production steps. Recent feasibility studies have reported the additive manufacturing of metallic, polymeric, and carbon-based composite BPs. As additive manufacturing of PEMFC BPs is still in the early stages of research and development, a thorough assessment of performance, scalability, and industrial readiness can clarify its current maturity and define future research directions. Accordingly, this study reviews recent progress in additive manufacturing of PEMFC BPs via powder bed fusion, material extrusion, photopolymerization, and jetting processes. Specifically, it discusses manufacturing capabilities and the characteristics of fabricated plates, evaluated both ex situ and in situ within fuel cells, and compares them with conventionally manufactured BPs. Among the processes assessed, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) delivers the optimal balance of geometric fidelity, surface finish, microstructural control, electrical conductivity, and corrosion resistance. After post-processing treatments, LPBF-fabricated BPs have demonstrated electrochemical performance that can exceed that of conventionally manufactured ones. This review also identifies challenges to the commercialization and scalability of printed BPs.
10.1016_j.electacta.2026.149474: Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) is a powerful analytical technique widely used in bioanalysis owing to its high sensitivity and low background signal. Given the biological and clinical importance of nucleic acid, ECL-based DNA detection has attracted considerable interest. In this study, we investigated the roles of DNA and a DNA-intercalating dye, SYBR Green I, in the [Ru(bpy) 3 ] 2+ ECL system. Despite its widespread use in nucleic acid detection, the influence of SYBR Green I on electrochemical and ECL processes has not been systematically investigated. Electrochemical analysis revealed that DNA promotes the oxidation of [Ru(bpy) 3 ] 2+ via catalytic interactions, however, this pathway contributes only weakly to ECL emission. In contrast, SYBR Green I significantly enhanced ECL intensity through a catalytic-like route, functioning as an effective coreactant. In the combined DNA–SYBR Green I system, intercalation of SYBR Green I into DNA partially suppressed the coreactant function of SYBR Green I. The ECL intensity decreased systematically with increasing DNA concentration. Furthermore, ECL generation was examined under spatially confined conditions using DNA gels. The results suggested that SYBR Green I contributes to ECL generation even within a DNA-bound state. These findings provide insight into the interplay between DNA, intercalating dyes, and [Ru(bpy) 3 ] 2+ , and establish a framework for designing ECL systems that integrate catalytic and coreactant pathways for bioanalytical applications.
